pedagogy.summary: At KS3, experimental probability is treated as relative frequency (frequency ÷ number of trials) serving as an ESTIMATE of an underlying probability — crucially, an estimate that is the ONLY route when a device is biased or its structure unknown (a drawing pin, a bent coin, a real-world event). The procedure is to record outcomes in a frequency table, compute relative frequencies, compare with theoretical values where they exist, and reason that the estimate improves as trials increase.
bestPractices: Compute relative frequency from the collected data (f ÷ n), not by restating a theoretical value
Use genuinely biased or unknown devices (drawing pin, bent coin, weighted die) so relative frequency is needed as an estimate, not just a check
Show the estimate stabilising as trials grow, by pooling data or simulation, to justify 'more trials → better estimate'
Explain discrepancies between experimental and theoretical as expected short-run variation, not error or bias
Use relative frequency × number of trials to predict expected frequencies in a new run
keyRepresentations: Frequency table with a relative-frequency (f ÷ n) column
Relative-frequency graph stabilising as trials increase
Experimental and theoretical values marked on the same 0-to-1 scale
Biased/unknown device whose probability can only be estimated
commonMisconceptions: Reporting the theoretical probability when asked for the experimental one, even for a biased/unknown device that has no calculable value
Concluding a device is biased (or fair) from too few trials (law of small numbers)
Thinking absolute counts must even out exactly with more trials (the 'due' fallacy) rather than relative frequency converging
Treating a small-sample relative frequency as a reliable estimate of the true probability

learn.summary: KS3 experimental probability treats relative frequency (frequency ÷ number of trials) as an ESTIMATE of an underlying probability — and the only available route when a device is biased or its structure unknown (a drawing pin, a bent coin, a weighted die, a real-world event), because its probability cannot be obtained from symmetry. Learners record outcomes in a frequency table, compute relative frequencies, compare with theoretical values where they exist, and reason that the estimate becomes more reliable as trials increase. The central insight: for a device with no symmetry-derived value, the settled relative frequency IS the best estimate, and that reliability is earned by running many trials rather than by trusting a short run.

activities.title: Drop a drawing pin and watch the estimate settle
feedback: If a learner writes P(point-up) = 1/2, point out that the pin is not symmetric, so there is nothing to calculate from symmetry; the probability must be estimated from the data — relative frequency is the only route.

If a learner declares the estimate settled after only 50 drops, show the relative frequency still shifting, extend the trials or pool data so it stabilises, and state that more trials give a more reliable estimate.

If a learner expects point-up and point-down counts to become exactly equal with more drops, distinguish relative frequency (which stabilises toward the true probability) from raw counts (which need not equalise); each drop is independent, so no result is ever 'due'.

If a learner reads the settled line (e.g. around 0.63 after many trials) and offers that as the estimate while noting that trusting the 50-drop figure would have been rash, affirm that the estimate earned its reliability from the number of trials.
activities.rationale: Experimental probability is relative frequency (frequency ÷ trials) estimated from data, and the estimate approaches the true value as trials grow — a short run such as 20 or 50 trials is not enough to rely on. A biased or unknown device removes the temptation to restate a theoretical value, so the learner must compute the estimate from their own data. Large trial counts are reached by pooling class data or by a simulator, since a single learner cannot physically drop a pin thousands of times.
sourceClaims: Experimental probability is the relative frequency (frequency of the event ÷ number of trials); it estimates the probability from data, and the more trials, the closer relative frequency gets to the true/theoretical value — a short run (e.g. 20 trials) is not enough to rely on.
learnerActions: Take a drawing pin (or a visibly bent coin) whose true point-up probability cannot be worked out from symmetry, and a frequency table with a relative-frequency (f ÷ n) column.
Drop the pin 50 times, recording point-up/point-down tallies, then compute relative frequency = point-up frequency ÷ 50.
State this relative frequency as your best estimate of the probability, and note explicitly that there is no theoretical value to calculate from symmetry because the pin is not symmetric.

Reach a much larger number of trials and recompute the relative frequency: pool the whole class's physical drops (same type of pin, dropped the same way onto the same kind of surface) to get into the hundreds, and/or use a hidden-true-probability pin/coin simulator (with the same frequency table and relative-frequency line) to reach 500 then 5000 trials quickly. Note that the simulator's settled value estimates the simulator's hidden probability, not your own pin's. Watch how the value jumps around early and then tends to settle near a steady figure.
Decide how much you would trust the 50-drop figure versus the large-trials figure, and say why.

Use your best estimate for your pin (from your own or pooled class drops of the same kind of pin) × number of trials to predict roughly how many point-ups to expect in a fresh run of, say, 200 drops, recognising that the actual count will vary around that prediction.
activities.intendedInsight: When a device is biased or its structure is unknown there is no formula to reach for — you must run trials. The relative frequency you read off IS your best estimate of a probability you could not calculate from symmetry, and that estimate earns its reliability from the number of trials: a 50-drop figure is rough and jumpy, while a settled line after many hundreds or thousands of trials is much more reliable, though still an estimate.

activities.title: Fair-device check: experimental versus theoretical on one scale
feedback: If a learner calls a small gap between experimental and theoretical values an 'error', reframe it as expected short-run variation that shrinks as trials grow.

If a learner judges the coin biased from a short run, explain that short runs vary a lot and gather more tosses or pool class data; for a fair coin the relative frequency tends to settle near 0.5 as trials increase (the law of large numbers), because early results get diluted by later ones rather than corrected.
activities.rationale: Comparing experimental relative frequency with theoretical probability on a shared scale makes convergence visible and names short-run variation, countering the belief that small samples must reflect the true probability. This complements the biased-device activity by showing both the case with and without a calculable value.
sourceClaims: Belief in the representativeness of small samples leads people to expect short runs to reflect the true probability and to over-trust small-sample estimates, and recency ('due') errors reflect a failure to treat trials as independent.
learnerActions: Toss an ordinary coin (or roll a fair die), record outcomes in a frequency table, and compute the relative frequency for each outcome.
Mark both your experimental relative frequency and the theoretical probability on the same 0-to-1 scale.
Explain a small gap between them as expected short-run variation rather than a mistake or evidence that the coin is biased.
Repeat with more tosses (or pool data) and see whether the experimental value tends to settle closer to the theoretical one.
activities.intendedInsight: Where a theoretical value does exist, relative frequency can be compared with it: discrepancies in a short run are normal variation, and the experimental value tends toward the theoretical as trials increase. This frames why, for a biased device with no symmetry-derived value, the relative frequency is all you have.

activities.title: Compute and judge reliability from given tables
feedback: If a learner picks the smaller sample as equally good, remind them that a larger number of trials makes the relative frequency a more reliable estimate.
If a learner tries to state a symmetry-based value for the bent coin, point out that an asymmetric device has no value obtainable from symmetry; only the data gives an estimate.
activities.rationale: Table-based computation and reliability judgements between two given samples assess relative-frequency fluency and sample-size reasoning. On their own they do not generate the data or the convergence, so they are best used after hands-on trials rather than as a substitute.
sourceClaims: Experimental probability is the relative frequency (frequency of the event ÷ number of trials); it estimates the probability from data, and the more trials, the closer relative frequency gets to the true/theoretical value — a short run (e.g. 20 trials) is not enough to rely on.
learnerActions: Given a completed frequency table, fill in the relative-frequency column (each outcome's frequency ÷ total trials).
Decide, for a bent coin, which of two samples (e.g. 30 trials versus 800 trials) gives the more reliable estimate of its bias, and justify your choice.
Explain in a sentence why you cannot calculate the bent coin's probability from symmetry.
activities.intendedInsight: Computing relative frequency from a table and judging sample-size reliability are skills that can be practised and checked — but they sit on top of the run-and-stabilise experience, which is where the meaning of 'more trials → better estimate' actually comes from.

constraints: Use a genuinely biased or unknown device (drawing pin, bent coin, weighted die, real-world event) for the core task, so relative frequency is needed as an estimate and not merely a check against a known answer.
Compute relative frequency from the collected data (f ÷ n); do not let the learner restate a theoretical value in its place.

The learner should actually run trials and watch the estimate stabilise — the convergence experience is the point, and this run-and-record-and-predict work is the curriculum evidence. Recognition-only or table-reading tasks assess the computation but do not themselves elicit the run-and-stabilise reasoning, so they should supplement rather than replace a hands-on run.
Make clear that relative frequency stabilises toward the true probability while raw counts need not equalise; avoid implying point-up and point-down counts must become equal.

Large trial counts (500/5000) are impractical to drop by hand: reach them with a hidden-true-probability simulator or by pooling class data; a physical single-learner run realistically reaches tens to a few hundred.

A live simulator (hidden-true-probability spinner or pin sampler with a frequency table, a relative-frequency line, and large-trial controls) and a physical pin/coin both deliver the estimating behaviour; neither is uniquely required. Physical tossing adds realism, while a simulator reaches large trial counts quickly — choose by what you can run, and pool class data if a physical run cannot reach many trials.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. The activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The legacy row's 'static image cannot teach this' and 'dialogue cannot generate the data' claims were softened to scoped affordance/limit statements: a fixed image cannot run trials and a conversation does not itself produce the convergence data, but these are not established comparative-efficacy findings. The '3D adds nothing' framing was likewise softened — physical tossing offers realism even though the 2D table and plot capture the estimating behaviour.

Example relative-frequency figures (0.62 jumping around at 50 drops, settling near 0.63 at 5000) are illustrative of a plausible biased pin, not measured values; actual values depend on the specific pin and conditions.

The claim that a drawing pin or bent coin has 'no calculable value' is treated as a practical KS3 simplification: a physical device has some true long-run probability that could in principle be modelled, but it cannot be obtained from symmetry and so must be estimated from data. Learner-facing wording was aligned to 'cannot be calculated from symmetry' rather than an unqualified 'no value exists'.

Activity 1's large trial counts were rescoped: a single-learner physical pin-drop cannot realistically reach 5000 drops, so the step routes 500/5000 trials through a simulator or pooled class data while keeping the stabilisation insight.

probeDeeper: Why can't you just calculate this probability the way you would for a fair die?
Your estimate after 50 drops is 0.6 — how much would you trust it? What would make you trust it more?
If you dropped it 5000 times, what would happen to the relative frequency? Would the counts of up and down become equal?
Two students estimate the pin: one from 30 drops, one from 800. Whose estimate would you use, and why?
assess.correctAnswer: A correct performance: records point-up/point-down in the table, computes relative frequency = point-up frequency ÷ 50, and offers THAT as the best estimate — recognising there is no theoretical value to calculate because the pin is not symmetric — while noting that 50 drops gives only a rough estimate and more trials would make it more reliable.

errorPatterns.pattern: Reports a theoretical value for a device that has none (says P(point-up) = 1/2 for a drawing pin)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Point out the pin is not symmetric, so there is nothing to calculate; the probability must be estimated from the data — relative frequency is the only route
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Gives 1/2 (or another symmetry-based value) instead of computing relative frequency from the drops

errorPatterns.pattern: Concludes the probability confidently from too few trials (law of small numbers)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show the relative frequency still shifting; extend trials or pool data so the estimate stabilises, and state that more trials give a more reliable estimate
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Declares the estimate settled after 50 drops with no caveat, or would judge fairness from a short run

errorPatterns.pattern: Thinks absolute counts must even out exactly with more trials (the 'due' fallacy) rather than relative frequency converging
errorPatterns.nextMove: Distinguish relative frequency (stabilises toward the true probability) from raw counts (need not equalise); each drop is independent
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Expects point-up and point-down counts to become equal, or says a result is 'due'

responseLevels.gap: States a theoretical value the device does not have, or treats a short-run relative frequency as exact; no sense that the estimate depends on trials
responseLevels.full: Estimates the probability by relative frequency from the data, recognises no theoretical value exists for the pin, treats 50 drops as limited, and states that more trials make the estimate more reliable as relative frequency stabilises
responseLevels.partial: Computes relative frequency from the data and knows it estimates the probability, but trusts a small sample without caveat, or expects counts to equalise — reports a number without reasoning about reliability

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Give the child a drawing pin (or a visibly bent coin) and a frequency table. Say: 'Find the probability that this pin lands point-up. Drop it 50 times, record the results, and tell me your best estimate of the probability — and whether 50 drops is enough.' (Set the task and WATCH — watch whether they compute relative frequency from their data or try to state a theoretical 1/2, how they treat the variation, and whether they judge 50 drops as limited.)
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Watching separates the child who estimates from their own data and hedges on 50 trials from one who states '1/2' (a theoretical value the pin does not have), treats the count as exact, or trusts 50 drops as definitive. Because the pin has no calculable probability, defaulting to theory is exposed immediately.
